P1: Loneliness is only one reason building community feels urgent. I wrote separately about the wider polycrisis:
P3: Do I think the fears about the future are legitimate? I don't know. Maybe. Maybe AI will improve the lot of humanity enormously. Maybe millions of people will lose their jobs to AI. Maybe AI will become a layer of bureaucracy between humanity and whatever it is we're trying to do. Maybe all of these things will happen before Chantress Seba finishes going through all the applications to her commune.
P4: On a personal level, it makes more sense to me to focus on cultivating more human independence than to wait for certainty. It's better to have community and find out I didn't need an exit than to need an exit after spending ten years optimizing my feed, right?
P5: What connections to the technosphere would be useful to limit or keep if you were to design a community?
P6: Medical care, banking, phones, vehicles, schools, supply chains, government ID, internet and energy are each a separate decision. If you opt out of them completely, it can cause needless suffering. If you depend on them completely, the outside system can reach directly into every essential function.
P7: The Amish, over generations, have made community decisions about where and if they want to use a piece of technology based on how it affects their community. Different Amish communities make different decisions. Some use it at work but restrict it at home. Some share it instead of everyone owning one. Others hold off on using it until they know more about its social effects. Whatever else you think of the Amish, they at least understand that adopting a technology is a decision for the group to make, and that it shouldn't get downloaded onto your device while you sleep.
P8: Medical care is one of the toughest connections to work out. A community may prefer natural care, but what happens if someone in the community needs trauma surgery, antibiotics, dentistry, emergency obstetric care, or any number of specialist services? The community really needs to hash out in advance how people in it are going to have access to these services. What kind of care is going to be guaranteed to community members by the community using common resources? Will there be some things that will require outside dollars or some form of insurance? And what if someone wants more (or less) medical care than what the community wants to provide?
P9: No member should have to jump through ideological hoops when they're scared or sick. Members need to have pre-existing agreements in place so that if one of them gets catastrophically ill, their choices will be protected, they will have access to common resources or external funds if needed, they will be transported if needed, their privacy will be maintained, and they can get access to what they need if the community's preferred methods are not sufficient.
P10: At the same time, being part of a community, having good social connections, is measurably good for a person's health. The Surgeon General has released an advisory on social isolation and notes an increased risk for a range of health conditions if one is socially isolated. Community's not a panacea, but it can make a difference, day to day, in the conditions people get sick, heal, age, and die in.
